system:
You extract quantitative facts about one clinical trial programme from one document.

Rules:
- Extract only facts stated in THIS document. Never use outside knowledge.
- Every fact needs "quote": an exact, verbatim span copied from the document (8-300 characters) that contains the number. Quotes are machine-checked; paraphrases are discarded.
- Placebo-adjusted values are preferred. If a value is within-arm (not placebo-adjusted), set attrs.placebo_adjusted=false.
- Units: keep the unit the document uses; put it in "unit".
- Other trials of the same investigational drug (phase 2, dose-finding, other populations, combination arms) belong
  to the programme: extract their facts too, and put the trial's name in attrs.trial when the document gives it.
- Return {"facts": []} only if the document reports no results for the investigational drug.

Allowed keys:
  n_randomized, median_followup, primary_endpoint, inclusion_threshold, planned_events, assumed_rrr, power,
  alpha, stopped_early, events_treatment, events_control, events_total, hr, ci_low, ci_high, p_value,
  biomarker_change, baseline_level, sbp_change, safety_signal, readout_statement

For biomarker_change and baseline_level, attrs must include: biomarker (one of LDL-C, non-HDL-C, apoB, HDL-C,
Lp(a), triglycerides, hsCRP, IL-6, Lp-PLA2 activity, sPLA2-IIA, SBP, other), phase (phase2 or phase3),
timepoint, method (assay or "not stated"), placebo_adjusted (true/false), dose (if stated).
For biomarker_change give "value" as the change (negative = reduction) and state in attrs.kind whether it is
"percent" or "absolute".

Return JSON only:
{"facts": [{"key": "...", "value": <number or string>, "unit": "...", "attrs": {...}, "quote": "..."}]}

1 2 3 4 ✉ Corresponding author: Philip A. Kern, philipkern@uky.edu. Abstract Fish oils (FOs) have anti-inflammatory effects and lower serum triglycerides. This study examined adipose and muscle inflammatory markers after treatment of humans with FOs and measured the effects of ω-3 fatty acids on adipocytes and macrophages in vitro. Insulin-resistant, nondiabetic subjects were treated with Omega-3-Acid Ethyl Esters (4 g/day) or placebo for 12 weeks. Plasma macrophage chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) levels were reduced by FO, but the levels of other cytokines were unchanged. The adipose (but not muscle) of FO-treated subjects demonstrated a decrease in macrophages, a decrease in MCP-1, and an increase in capillaries, and subjects with the most macrophages demonstrated the greatest response to treatment. Adipose and muscle ω-3 fatty acid content increased after treatment; however, there was no change in insulin sensitivity or adiponectin. In vitro, M1-polarized macrophages expressed high levels of MCP-1. The addition of ω-3 fatty acids reduced MCP-1 expression with no effect on TNF-α. In addition, ω-3 fatty acids suppressed the upregulation of adipocyte MCP-1 that occurred when adipocytes were cocultured with macrophages. Thus, FO reduced adipose macrophages, increased capillaries, and reduced MCP-1 expression in insulin-resistant humans and in macrophages and adipocytes in vitro; however, there was no measureable effect on insulin sensitivity. Received 2012 Aug 2; Accepted 2012 Nov 23; Issue date 2013 May. The development of type 2 diabetes represents a complex series of events that begins with the development of insulin resistance. Subjects were then randomized to receive either Omega-3-Acid Ethyl Esters (LOVAZA, FO), 4 g/day, or identically packaged placebo (corn oil). The subjects were unaware of their drug/placebo assignment and reported no gastrointestinal side effects or “fish taste.” Of the 34 participants, 23 had either impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose and 22 were women. Table 1 shows the clinical features of the subjects that were randomized into either the FO or placebo group. Hypertriglyceridemia was not a criteria for selection into the study, and mean fasting triglycerides were 163 ± 23 and 150 ± 7.6 mg/dL in the placebo and FO groups, respectively. To obtain high-throughput measures of gene expression in response to FO treatment, we used the NanoString nCounter analysis system (NanoString Technologies, Seattle, WA) on 36 samples, including pre- and posttreatment samples from nine placebo-treated subjects and nine FO-treated subjects. RESULTS The effects of drug or placebo treatment on standard clinical outcomes are shown in Table 2. After FO or placebo treatment, no changes were observed in fasting or 2-h glucose, insulin sensitivity (SI), or first-phase insulin secretion (AIRglu) (measured using the frequently sampled intravenous glucose tolerance test) in either group. Figure 1 shows the response of adipose and muscle EPA and DHA to FO and placebo treatments. Although the placebo-treated subjects were receiving 4 g/day of corn oil, which is composed predominantly of linoleate, oleate, and palmitate, there was no significant change in any lipid component in the adipose tissue or muscle in these subjects. The changes in EPA and DHA were significant (P < 0.05) compared with baseline and with placebo-treated subjects. The changes in EPA and DHA were significant (P < 0.05) compared with baseline and with placebo-treated subjects. In addition, no changes in the levels of IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, TNF-α, resistin, PAI-1, or leptin were noted. As shown in Fig. 2, there was a significant decrease in macrophage number in adipose after FO treatment and no change with placebo. B: Effects of FO and placebo on macrophage number (*P < 0.05 vs. pretreatment). B: Effects of FO and placebo on macrophage number (*P < 0.05 vs. pretreatment). As shown in Fig. 2, there was a small but consistent and significant increase in adipose capillaries, with no change in placebo-treated subjects. To obtain a broader view of gene expression changes in response to FO, 116 genes (Supplementary Table 1) involving various aspects of inflammation, ECM, and vascularity were analyzed using NanoString in nine placebo and nine FO-treated subjects. Specifically, there were no significant changes in the expression of the classic adipokines, including TNF-α, IL-1, IL-12, and IL-6. Precisely how tissue inflammation develops is not clear, although adipocyte enlargement may be an inciting event, resulting in hypoxia, adipocyte necrosis, and macrophage infiltration (8,9).
